entry.evidence: forecasting changes in behavior within an ongoing eruptive episode remains challenging and requires greater understanding of individual systems

sequences.source_document: Brill et al. 2022, Bull Volcanol 84:37, published PDF

steps.action: The authors frame the problem of understanding behaviour within a long-lived open-vent eruption at Fuego, where paroxysms are hard to forecast.
steps.quote: forecasting changes in behavior within an ongoing eruptive episode remains challenging and requires greater understanding of individual systems

steps.action: The authors take over their own earlier catalogues of repeating LP events (2008-2015) and the crack model that explains them.
steps.quote: Brill et al. (2018) reported on a suite of repeating LP events which occurred during 2012

steps.action: The authors take over the group's earlier 2008-2009 description of three vent-specific VLP event types (Lyons and Waite 2011; Waite et al. 2013).
steps.quote: Waite and others (2013) describe 3 types of VLP events

steps.action: The authors designed a 2012 temporary network to add azimuthal coverage south and southeast of the vent, where the VLP wavefield had not been sampled.
steps.quote: In 2012, we installed another temporary seismic network at Fuego volcano to further investigate the VLP events

steps.action: The authors deployed nine broadband stations, infrasound arrays and cameras in January 2012, then identified VLP events from visual emissions, filtered records and hand-picked amplitudes.
steps.quote: We deployed instruments from 13 to 23 January 2012

steps.action: No VLP signal appeared on the southern stations, so the authors tried linear and phase-weighted stacks and a match filter; neither recovered network-wide signals.
steps.quote: Unfortunately, no coherent VLP signal was recorded by any of these southern stations

steps.action: The authors compared the 2012 events with the 2008-2009 types and found all three types, plus vent-crossing variants.
steps.quote: we did observe all of the three event types reported in Waite et al. (2013) during 2012

steps.action: The authors expanded the classification with types 1A and 2A, keeping vent of origin as the primary grouping factor (Table 1).
steps.quote: deferring to the vent of origin as the main factor in grouping emission events

steps.action: The authors compared amplitudes and peak periods across years and types: 2012 events are smaller, and stacked peak frequencies match 2009, but individual periods overlap widely (Figs. 3-4).
steps.quote: the largest events from 2012 are on par with the smallest events observed in 2009

steps.action: The authors asked whether the 2012 VLP events separate by signal characteristics (emergent or impulsive) rather than by vent.
steps.quote: we wondered if the 2012 VLP events might be better differentiated according to the signal characteristics

steps.action: The authors cross-correlated all visually identified 2012 VLP events with the GISMO Correlation Toolbox and clustered them in a dendrogram (Fig. 5); event types intersperse.
steps.quote: There is no hard line between impulsive and emergent

steps.action: The authors rejected discrete vent-specific VLP categories, since no signal characteristic identifies the vent of origin, in favour of a continuum.
steps.quote: we could not find any combination of seismic signal characteristics like frequency content or waveform shape that uniquely identified the vent of origin

steps.action: The authors built a template from a phase-weighted stack of 111 type 2 events and ran a 160-s moving-window match filter (threshold 0.7) over 2008-2015 data from co-located stations; it found events in every year (Fig. 3).
steps.quote: The persistence of this individual type of event based on signal characteristics alone is remarkable for its longevity

steps.action: As a check, the authors noted that the 2009 match-filter detections include the event Lyons and Waite (2011) used for their moment-tensor inversion.
steps.quote: one of them corresponding to the individual event which Lyons and Waite (2011) used for their inversion

steps.action: The authors kept the claim that the VLP centroid mechanism and location stayed largely unchanged despite paroxysms between 2012 and 2015.
steps.quote: the VLP centroid mechanism and location remain largely unchanged

steps.action: The authors took over the group's earlier inverted source (a dike feeding a sill about 300 m below the vent) and its tilt-based pressurization interpretation.
steps.quote: a steeply (65°) dipping dike feeding a shallowly (35°) dipping sill

steps.action: The authors added to the conduit model that the breaking seal may begin below the conduit split, based on closely spaced summit and flank emissions in 2012.
steps.quote: One addition we can make to this model is that the seal which is breaking may at times begin below the split

steps.action: The authors mapped 2011-2015 vent positions from Google Earth imagery and compared them with the crater states of Diaz-Moreno et al. (2020): shallow pathways are ephemeral while the deeper system stays stable.
steps.quote: The 2012 observation period would fall into a time with an ephemeral cone based on Google Earth Imagery (Fig. 2)

steps.action: The authors hypothesized that a stable conduit geometry lets ascending magma self-organize into volatile- and crystal-rich and -poor zones that group explosions.
steps.quote: may allow for a kind of self-organization into zones with more volatiles and crystals and zones with less

steps.action: The authors checked system stability with independent data, daily RSAM from the permanent FG3 station for 2007-2015 (Fig. 6).
steps.quote: We present two other measures of relative systemic stability over our 7-year observation period from 2008 to 2015

steps.action: The authors checked stability with annual mean SO2 emission rates from OMI (Fig. 7), arguing Fuego dominates over the possible Pacaya contribution because of vent altitude.
steps.quote: remained steady at ~ 200–300 t/d between 2008 and 2015

steps.action: The authors updated the conduit model (Fig. 8): the conduit split lies above the VLP centroid, the dike-sill constriction sorts magma, a mush plug and margin cracks form, and small supply-rate changes drive regime shifts.
steps.quote: the point where the conduit splits to feed the individual vents be located above the VLP source centroid

steps.action: The authors compared the model with earlier findings: explosion clustering with Poisson degassing (Brill et al. 2018), dominant processes (Castro-Escobar 2017), and pyroclast residence times (Lloyd et al. 2013).
steps.quote: This sorting of the magma at shallow depths explains the clustering of explosive events

steps.action: The authors concluded that VLP-source persistence, RSAM and SO2 show a stable conduit geometry from 2008 to 2015, with a change around 2015-2016.
steps.quote: The persistence of the process generating these VLP signals indicates that the conduit geometry has also been stable throughout at least this 8-year period.

end.claim: The VLP source, and hence the deeper conduit geometry, at Fuego remained stable for at least 2008-2015, supported by stable RSAM and SO2 emissions, while shallow vent pathways varied.

decisive_move.sentence: The 2008-2015 match-filter catalogue, built from a 2012 type 2 template, established that the same VLP waveform recurred in every deployment year, which grounds the stability claim.

gates.evidence: The 2012 network was designed to sample the VLP wavefield to the south (p. 2, 5), but no stated hypothesis directed acquisition. The match filter could have failed to find events in other years, and the dendrogram could have separated events by vent (p. 6-7), so the claims faced checks they could fail. However, the conduit model is fitted qualitatively and not tested. The correlation threshold of 0.7 and the template were chosen with no statement that they were fixed in advance (p. 7).

novelty_claims.quote: Each of these newly observed behaviors
Seismic signals that had only been associated with one vent in prior years are observed at both vents in 2012.
We use these signals to inform an updated model of shallow conduit dynamics

limits: No review file was supplied; the acknowledgements say the revision improved the paper, but what changed is unknown. The Electronic Supplementary Material (event table, detailed classification, southern-station noise analysis) was not supplied. The southern stations recorded no VLP signal, and the source of their noise is left unexplained. The 2014 record covers only 1.75 days. The 2015 upper amplitudes are likely an instrumentation artifact. The SO2 trend lies within measurement uncertainty and may include Pacaya. The match-filter threshold and template were not varied (no robustness test). Sub-claims at different statuses: the continuum interpretation (VLP character governed by small magma-supply changes) is best_explanation and untested; the updated conduit model (split above the VLP centroid, self-organization, mush plug, cracks) is best_explanation, supported by consistency with prior work only (inference). The inherited VLP source location is an estimate taken from Lyons and Waite (2011) and was not re-inverted here.

disagreements.target: Waite et al. (2013) vent-based classification of VLP event types
disagreements.support: In 2012 both waveform styles came from both vents, and the dendrogram and period histograms show no boundaries between types.
disagreements.quote: We suggest that all these events are part of a continuum of VLP activity

disagreements.target: Conduit model of Lyons and Waite (2011)
disagreements.support: Closely spaced summit and flank emissions and vent-crossing waveforms imply that the seal breaks below the split and the split lies above the VLP centroid.
disagreements.quote: One addition we can make to this model is that the seal which is breaking may at times begin below the split
